lessons.title: Separating Personal and Business Money
lessons.body:
When you run a tissue and paper products business, money flows in and out constantly. If you mix your personal money with business money, you will never know if your business is actually making a profit. Start by opening a separate bank account or mobile money wallet for your business. In Kenya, use M-Pesa with a separate SIM card; in Nigeria, use a dedicated bank account or Opay wallet. Even if you operate informally, keep a separate cash box for business cash. 

Every time you sell a pack of tissues, that money goes into the business account. When you need to buy raw materials or pay for transport, you take from that account. If you need personal money, pay yourself a fixed salaryâsay 10,000 shillings per weekâand record it as an expense. That way, you can see if the business can afford to pay you. 

A simple method: Use two envelopes. One for business cash, one for personal cash. At the end of each day, count both. If you find yourself borrowing from the business envelope to buy personal items, you are stealing from your business. Instead, write down the amount as a loan from the business to you, and repay it. 

Separating money also helps when applying for loans or grants. Lenders want to see clean records. If your business account shows regular sales and expenses, you are more likely to get funding. Start today: open that separate account, even if it is just a mobile wallet. Your business will thank you.

lessons.title: Using a Simple Cash Book or Mobile App for Record Keeping
lessons.body:
You don't need accounting software to keep good records. A simple exercise book can work as a cash book. Draw five columns: Date, Description, Money In, Money Out, and Balance. Every time you receive money, write it in 'Money In'. Every time you spend, write it in 'Money Out'. At the end of each day, calculate the balance: previous balance plus money in minus money out. 

For example, on Monday you start with 5,000 KSh. You sell 20 packs of tissues at 100 KSh each, so you write 2,000 in Money In. You buy glue for 500 KSh, so you write 500 in Money Out. Your new balance is 6,500 KSh. Do this every day without fail. 

If you prefer a mobile app, try 'M-Pesa Business' or 'Wave' for basic tracking. For a free, simple app, use 'Cash Book' on Android or 'Money Manager Expense & Budget'. These apps let you record transactions on your phone. They automatically calculate balances and even show you charts of where your money goes. 

Whichever method you choose, keep it consistent. Record every transaction, no matter how small. At the end of the week, total your Money In and Money Out. This weekly summary is the foundation for tracking profit. Remember, the goal is not to be perfect but to be honest. If you forget to record a sale, your records lie to you. So make it a habit: after every sale or purchase, record it immediately.

lessons.title: Tracking Sales, Expenses, and Profit Weekly
lessons.body:
To know if your tissue business is making money, you must track sales, expenses, and profit every week. Set aside one hour each Sunday evening to review your cash book or app. 

First, total your sales for the week. For example, if you sold 500 packs of tissues at 100 KSh each, your total sales are 50,000 KSh. Next, total your expenses: raw materials (paper, glue, packaging), transport, rent, airtime, and any wages you paid yourself. Suppose expenses are 35,000 KSh. Your profit is 50,000 minus 35,000 = 15,000 KSh. 

But don't stop there. Calculate your profit margin: profit divided by sales, times 100. In this case, 15,000 / 50,000 = 30%. A healthy tissue business often has a margin of 20-40%. If your margin is lower, look for ways to reduce costs or increase prices. 

Also, track your sales by product. Maybe toilet paper sells faster than facial tissues. If so, focus more on toilet paper. Write these numbers in a notebook or a simple spreadsheet on your phone. Over time, you'll see trends. For instance, sales may drop during school holidays. Knowing this helps you plan. 

Finally, compare this week's profit to last week's. If profit is falling, investigate why. Maybe a competitor opened nearby, or your supplier increased prices. By tracking weekly, you catch problems early. This simple habit is what separates thriving businesses from those that close down.

lessons.title: Managing Credit Sales to Trusted Customers
lessons.body:
Selling on credit can grow your tissue business, but it can also destroy it if you are not careful. Credit means you give goods now and get paid later. Only offer credit to customers you trustâthose who have bought from you for at least three months and always pay on time. 

Set clear terms: for example, payment within 7 days. Write it down. Use a credit book or a notebook to record: customer name, date, items taken, amount owed, and due date. For each credit sale, get the customer's phone number and, if possible, their national ID number. This reduces the risk of them disappearing. 

When payment is due, send a polite reminder via SMS or WhatsApp. For example: 'Hello Mary, your payment of 2,000 KSh for tissues is due today. Please pay via M-Pesa to 0712345678.' If they don't pay, follow up with a call. If they still don't pay after two weeks, stop giving them credit until they clear the debt. 

Never let one customer owe you more than 10% of your weekly sales. If your weekly sales are 50,000 KSh, the maximum credit to one customer should be 5,000 KSh. Also, keep a list of bad debtors and share it with other local suppliers if appropriateâthis encourages payment. 

Remember, a sale is not a sale until the money is in your pocket. Cash is king. Use credit strategically to build loyalty with your best customers, but never let it get out of hand.

lessons.title: Saving for Equipment Upgrades and Emergencies
lessons.body:
Your tissue business will need new equipmentâa sealing machine, a better weighing scale, or a delivery bicycle. And emergencies happen: a machine breaks down, a family member gets sick, or a supplier demands cash upfront. You must save for these. 

Open a separate savings account or mobile wallet for your business savings. Every week, after calculating your profit, transfer a fixed percentageâat least 10%âinto that savings. For example, if your weekly profit is 15,000 KSh, save 1,500 KSh. Do this before you spend on anything else. 

Set specific goals. If a sealing machine costs 30,000 KSh, you need to save 1,500 KSh per week for 20 weeks. Write the goal on your wall: 'Sealing machine by December.' This keeps you motivated. 

For emergencies, aim to save three months of business expenses. If your monthly expenses are 100,000 KSh, your emergency fund target is 300,000 KSh. This may take time, but start small. Even 500 KSh per week adds up. 

Use a locked savings account or a SACCO where you cannot easily withdraw. In Kenya, M-Shwari or a chama savings group can help. In Nigeria, use a PiggyVest or a local cooperative. 

When you dip into savings for an emergency, repay it as soon as possible. Treat your savings as a loan to yourself. This discipline will keep your business stable and ready to grow.

lessons.title: Understanding Basic Taxes and Licenses for Your Business
lessons.body:
Many small business owners fear taxes, but understanding them protects you from fines and helps you grow. In most African countries, if your business is small, you may qualify for a simplified tax regime. For example, in Kenya, the Turnover Tax (TOT) is 1% of gross sales for businesses with annual sales below 5 million KSh. In Nigeria, the presumptive tax for small businesses is often a flat fee based on your turnover. 

First, register your business. In Kenya, register with the Business Registration Service and get a KRA PIN. In Nigeria, register with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) and get a TIN. This makes you official and allows you to open a bank account and apply for loans. 

Next, get a local business permit from your county or municipality. This is usually paid annually and costs between 2,000 and 10,000 KSh depending on your location and size. Keep the receipt. 

For taxes, keep accurate records of all sales and expenses. You will need them to file returns. In Kenya, file your TOT returns monthly via iTax. In Nigeria, file with FIRS or your state internal revenue service. If you are unsure, visit your local tax office and ask for helpâthey often have officers to assist small businesses. 

Also, check if you need specific licenses for tissue products. In some countries, you may need a health certificate or a standards mark from the Bureau of Standards. This ensures your tissues meet quality requirements. 

Don't ignore taxes. The penalties can close your business. Instead, budget for them: set aside a small percentage of each sale for tax. When you pay on time, you build a good reputation and avoid stress.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Managing Money and Records for Tissue & Paper Businesses

Whether you convert jumbo reels into toilet rolls, trade in paper towels, or run a small tissue converting unit, money moves fast. Cash comes in over the counter, goes out to suppliers, and often gets mixed with household money. This Practical Reference brings together all six lessons in the module into one working document you can print, pin to the wall, and use daily. It is written for African micro and small enterprises â from Kumasi to Kampala, from Lagos to Lusaka â where most transactions are still cash or mobile money, and where trust and record keeping decide whether a business survives.

1. Separating Personal and Business Money

The single most common reason small tissue businesses fail is not low sales â it is mixing household money with business money. When the same pocket or mobile wallet funds school fees, stock purchases, and airtime, you can never know whether the business is profitable. Open a dedicated bank account or mobile money wallet for the business. Pay yourself a fixed monthly salary (even a small one), and treat all other withdrawals as a loan that must be repaid. This one habit transforms how you see your business.

2. Using a Simple Cash Book or Mobile App

You do not need accounting software. A hardcover exercise book with five columns â Date, Description, Money In, Money Out, Balance â is enough. Every sale and every expense gets a line. If you prefer digital, apps such as Wave, Kippa, or Moniepoint (Nigeria), M-PESA statements (Kenya/Tanzania), or MTN MoMo / Airtel Money transaction histories work well. The rule is simple: if it is not written down, it did not happen.

3. Tracking Sales, Expenses, and Profit Weekly

Weekly tracking turns guessing into decision-making. Every Sunday evening, total your sales, total your expenses, and calculate profit. If profit is falling, check whether it is a price problem, a cost problem, or a theft/wastage problem. For tissue converters, watch reel prices and glue costs closely â they move fast and eat margins.

Layout adapted from the ILO SIYB Improve Your Business record-keeping module. Source: ILO SIYB.

4. Managing Credit Sales to Trusted Customers

Credit sales grow revenue but destroy businesses when unmanaged. Set a written rule: a customer can only buy on credit after three successful cash purchases. Keep a simple credit ledger with name, phone number, amount owed, date due, and amount paid. Send a polite reminder one day before the due date. Never let one customer's debt exceed 10% of your monthly sales.

5. Saving for Equipment Upgrades and Emergencies

Tissue converting equipment â rewinders, log saws, sealing machines â is expensive. Save a fixed percentage of weekly profit (10â15%) into a separate savings wallet or a chama/sacco/VSLA group. Aim for two funds: an Equipment Fund for growth and an Emergency Fund covering at least one month of expenses. Village Savings and Loan Associations (VSLAs) are the most accessible savings vehicle for African micro-entrepreneurs â over 10 million members across sub-Saharan Africa.

Percentages adapted from the ILO Financial Education for Small Business curriculum and CARE International VSLA methodology. Sources: ILO SIYB; CARE VSLA.

6. Understanding Basic Taxes and Licences

Every African country has a simplified tax regime for small businesses. In Kenya, the Turnover Tax applies to businesses with turnover below KES 5 million. In Nigeria, small companies (turnover below â¦25 million) enjoy a lower Companies Income Tax rate and simplified filing. In Ghana, the GRA operates a presumptive tax for small businesses. In Uganda, URA's Small Business Tax regime applies below UGX 150 million turnover. You must also hold a valid trade licence from your local council or municipality. Register early â penalties compound.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Do Not Ignore Tax Notices

Ignoring tax authority letters, SMS reminders, or licence renewal deadlines can lead to business closure, asset seizure, and personal liability. In several African jurisdictions, unpaid turnover tax accrues penalties of 5â25% plus interest. If you receive a notice you do not understand, visit the nearest tax office or a free business development services (BDS) centre the same week. Never pay a "facilitator" who promises to reduce your tax â this is bribery and can lead to prosecution. Use only official channels.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Separate accounts: Business money in its own bank account, mobile wallet, or cash box â never mixed with household cash.
  2. Daily entries: Every sale and expense recorded the same day in a cash book or mobile app.
  3. Weekly review: Every Sunday, total sales, expenses, and profit; compare to your target.
  4. Credit rules: Written credit limit per customer; ledger kept; reminders sent one day before due date.
  5. Savings discipline: 15% of weekly profit split between Equipment Fund and Emergency Fund.
  6. Tax calendar: Know your filing dates; keep 10% of profit reserved for tax and licences.
  7. Licence renewal: Mark renewal dates on the wall calendar three months in advance.
  8. Owner's salary: Pay yourself a fixed amount monthly â do not draw randomly from the till.

Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • ILO Start and Improve Your Business (SIYB) â free training materials and record-keeping tools
  • CARE International â Village Savings and Loan Association (VSLA) methodology and toolkits
  • OECD â Tax and Development resources on simplified SME tax regimes in Africa
  • African Development Bank â Financial Inclusion for SMEs in Africa
  • GSMA Mobile for Development â Mobile money record keeping for micro-enterprises

This Practical Reference is part of the RISE AFRICA Skills course Tissues & Paper Products â Module: Managing Money and Records. Use it alongside the six lesson pages, and update your figures weekly.

quiz.q: Why should you separate personal and business money?
options: A) To make it easier to steal from the business
B) To know if your business is actually making a profit
quiz.explanation: Separating money helps you track business performance accurately.

quiz.q: What is a simple tool for record keeping mentioned in the lesson?
options: A) A computer with expensive software
B) A cash book with columns for Money In, Money Out, and Balance
C) A diary for personal thoughts
quiz.explanation: A cash book is a simple, effective record-keeping tool.

quiz.q: If you start with 5,000 KSh, sell 2,000 KSh, and spend 500 KSh, what is your new balance?
Which mobile app is suggested for record keeping?
quiz.explanation: Cash Book is a free Android app for tracking transactions.

quiz.q: How often should you review your sales, expenses, and profit?
quiz.explanation: Weekly tracking helps catch problems early.

quiz.q: If sales are 50,000 KSh and expenses 35,000 KSh, what is the profit margin?
What should you do if profit is falling?
options: B) Investigate why and take action
quiz.explanation: Investigating falling profit helps you fix issues.

quiz.q: Who should you offer credit sales to?
options: B) Only trusted customers with a good payment history
quiz.explanation: Credit should be limited to trustworthy customers.

quiz.q: What is a good credit term to set?
options: D) Payment whenever they feel like it
quiz.explanation: Short terms reduce risk of non-payment.

quiz.q: What should you do if a customer doesn't pay after two weeks?
options: B) Stop giving credit until they clear the debt
quiz.explanation: Stopping credit encourages payment and protects your business.

quiz.q: What is the maximum credit you should give to one customer?
quiz.explanation: Limiting credit to 10% of weekly sales reduces risk.

quiz.q: Why is cash considered king?
options: A) Because a sale is not a sale until money is in your pocket
C) Because it's easy to steal
D) Because banks don't like cash
quiz.explanation: Cash ensures you actually have the money to run the business.

quiz.q: How much of your profit should you save weekly?
quiz.explanation: Saving at least 10% builds funds for equipment and emergencies.

quiz.q: What is a good emergency fund target?
options: B) Three months of business expenses
quiz.explanation: Three months of expenses covers most emergencies.

quiz.q: Where can you save that makes withdrawal difficult?
options: B) A locked savings account or SACCO
quiz.explanation: Locked accounts or SACCOs help you avoid impulsive withdrawals.

quiz.q: What should you do if you dip into savings for an emergency?
options: B) Repay it as soon as possible
quiz.explanation: Treating savings as a loan to yourself maintains discipline.

quiz.q: In Kenya, what is the Turnover Tax rate for small businesses?
quiz.explanation: TOT is 1% of gross sales for qualifying small businesses.

quiz.q: What is the first step to formalize your business?
options: A) Register with the relevant authorities and get a tax PIN
D) Move to a new location
quiz.explanation: Registration and tax PIN are basic requirements.

quiz.q: Where do you get a local business permit?
options: A) From your county or municipality
quiz.explanation: Local permits are issued by county or municipal offices.

quiz.q: Why should you keep accurate records for taxes?
options: D) To confuse the tax office
quiz.explanation: Accurate records are needed to file tax returns.

quiz.q: What might you need for tissue products in some countries?
options: A) A health certificate or standards mark
quiz.explanation: Health certificates or standards marks ensure quality compliance.

quiz.q: What happens if you ignore taxes?
options: B) You may face penalties that can close your business
quiz.explanation: Tax penalties can be severe and harm your business.

quiz.q: How can you budget for taxes?
options: A) Set aside a small percentage of each sale
quiz.explanation: Setting aside a percentage ensures you have money for taxes.

quiz.q: What is one benefit of paying taxes on time?
options: A) You build a good reputation
C) You avoid all future taxes
quiz.explanation: Timely tax payment builds trust with authorities.

quiz.q: What should you do if you are unsure about tax filing?
options: A) Visit your local tax office for help
B) Guess and hope for the best
quiz.explanation: Tax offices often have officers to assist small businesses.

quiz.q: In Nigeria, which agency registers businesses?
quiz.explanation: CAC is responsible for business registration in Nigeria.

quiz.q: What is a presumptive tax?
options: A) A flat fee based on turnover for small businesses
B) A tax on profits only
D) A tax on personal income
quiz.explanation: Presumptive tax simplifies taxation for small businesses.

quiz.q: Why is separating business and personal money important for loans?
options: A) Lenders want to see clean records
C) It makes you look rich
D) It's a legal requirement always
quiz.explanation: Clean records show lenders your business is creditworthy.

quiz.q: What is a chama?
quiz.explanation: A chama is a community savings group common in East Africa.

quiz.q: What should you do after every sale or purchase?
quiz.explanation: Immediate recording ensures accuracy in your records.
